extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of comparative politics / American government
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and dimensions for judging the strengths and faults of American democracy as discussed in a political-science/textbook excerpt. Focuses on institutional design, public character, and social forces that affect governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative–administrative separation
rubrics_metrics.description: “The legislatures are disjoined from the administrative offices.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that separation of executive from legislature can have advantages but can also prevent legislatures from securing the benefits of experienced administrators; disjunction may impede effective choice and application of best means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of legislative representation
rubrics_metrics.description: “The members of legislatures are not selected for their ability or experience, but are, two-thirds of them little above the average citizen, being in many places so chosen as to represent rather the local machine than the people.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates representative bodies by how members are selected (merit/experience vs. machine/localism), the respect/trust they command, and whether selection processes encourage capable public service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public attitude toward expertise and delegated power
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic self-confidence may pass into a jealousy of delegated power, an undervaluing of skill and knowledge, a belief that any citizen is good enough for any political work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures the degree to which popular sovereignty undervalues professional competence; considers whether democratic temperament discourages elites from public service and lowers standards for high office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of strong local self-government on national standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Excellence of rural local self-government has lowered the conception of national government; ordinary citizens imagine national offices like larger local offices and elect similar types of persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses whether success at local levels produces complacency or lowered expectations for national leaders and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spoils system and machine politics
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Spoils System reminds us of the Machine and the whole organization of Rings and Bosses.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considers number and frequency of elections and party-reward practices that create patronage, machines, rings, and bosses; notes these are not necessarily intrinsic to democracy and may be removable by reform (e.g., reducing patronage, reforming election law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of wealth (money power / corporate influence)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Wealth, skilfully used, can overcome ... the public virtue ... supplies the funds for maintaining party organizations and defraying the enormous costs of electoral campaigns, and demands in return sometimes a high administrative post ... a clause in a tariff bill, sometimes a lucrative contract.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates how wealth distorts democratic incentives: buying influence, funding parties, tainting elections (including via indirect corporate structures), and pressing for legislation or contracts. Notes protections (criminal justice, electoral punishment) and institutional remedies (better ballot and election laws).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corruption and its remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Corruption has appeared historically (e.g., English Parliament under Walpole); growth of intelligence, penalties for bribery, and extinction of small constituencies have reduced electoral corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Looks at presence of bribery, tampering with returns, and corrupt influence; examines legal and institutional remedies (secret ballot, election laws, penalties) and historical trajectories showing corruption can be diminished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dignity of public life and quality of leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: “The want of dignity in public life, prominence of inferior men, and the absence of distinguished figures.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses public life for dignity, presence of capable, enlightened leaders, and whether the political culture produces figures who can inspire and lead beyond the mass. Notes democracy especially needs great leaders to correct fatalistic tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence (or presence) of ochlocracy / mob-rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The commonest old charge against democracy was that it passed into ochlocracy; the text argues this has not happened in America—mob-rule features do not appear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates whether the system shows features of mob-rule or maintains institutional restraints; distinguishes mob-rule from other faults like professional political classes or plutocratic influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability of institutions (durability)
rubrics_metrics.description: “As one test ... its capacity for reaching a great age ... The Federal Constitution has been... an almost sacred thing ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considers attachment of the people to constitutional form, ability to survive crises (e.g., Civil War), and reluctance to radical institutional change; stability provides trust and resilience but may impede needed reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for and obedience to the law (legality)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Feeling the law to be their own work, the people are disposed to obey the law.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures law-abiding habits deriving from direct participation (seeing statutes as 'made by themselves'), acceptance of legal procedures (even judicial nullification of popular votes), and examples (Mormons, misgoverned cities) showing preference for constitutional/legal solutions over arbitrary force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and consistency of political ideas (preference for uniformity)
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is a broad simplicity about the political ideas of the people, and a courageous consistency in carrying them out in practice ... they prefer certainty and uniformity to the advantages which might occasionally be gained by deviation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates the population's attachment to clear, uniform principles (e.g., freedom of the press) and willingness to tolerate abuses for overall benefits. Notes this yields steadiness but can allow evils to persist too long.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance of liberty / willingness to bear abuses
rubrics_metrics.description: On the boundless freedom of the press: abuses must be borne with and left to the sentiment of the people and the private law of libel to deal with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses trade-offs between liberty and short-term harms; examines cases (Ku Klux outrages, labor boycotts) where restraint and trust in constitutional processes were preferred to violent or extraordinary remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited arbitrary administrative power (legal constraint on officials)
rubrics_metrics.description: American government, relying very little on officials, has the merit of arming them with little power of arbitrary interference; powers of each authority are carefully and closely restricted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates the administrative structure for legal limitations on discretionary power, reliance on law rather than inquisitorial administrative powers, and distribution of functions that assist rather than supplant private enterprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of entrenched class struggles and diffusion of property
rubrics_metrics.description: “There are no struggles between privileged and unprivileged orders ... for political purposes classes scarcely exist ... the poorer class have ... political power, equal civil rights, a career open to all citizens alike ... gratuitous higher as well as elementary education.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses social equality for political stability: diffusion of property and broad access to rights reduces class antagonism; measures whether labour–capital conflicts are framed as class struggles or targeted at corporate abuse of privileges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public spirit: civic duty, self-help, and practical judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The average native American shows intelligence in his political judgments, a strong sense of the duty of giving a vote, and a spirit of alertness and enterprise which has made him self-helpful above all other men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates civic virtues (participation, prudence, enterprise) that sustain democratic institutions and public policy; considers the role of public opinion and popular temperament in enabling lawful and effective governance.
